item.text:
The draft has several potentially dispositive defects, particularly the chronology, statutory authority, imminence showing, and irreversible relief without a prior hearing. This review treats the quoted statutory language as supplied; the full Act, corrections legislation, and Commission rules would need to be checked before making definitive procedural claims.

1. **Caption, cover sheet, and paragraph 3(d)—Identify the legal respondent.** “OpenAI” may not identify the particular legal entity that develops, deploys, owns, or controls each model. Name the relevant entities and establish their relationship to the systems and their ability to comply with the requested order.

2. **Title and paragraphs 3(b), 4—Obsolete statutory citation.** On the draft’s own account, former Section 112(c) has become Section 212(c). Verify the redesignation’s effective date, cite the operative provision, and confirm that the quotation remains current.

3. **Paragraph 4 and prayer (b)—The quoted authority does not authorize deletion.** The provision permits suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days, not destruction of model assets. Respondent will argue that permanent deletion exceeds the Commission’s authority; identify separate statutory authority or change the requested remedy.

4. **Paragraphs 1, 9 and prayer—The petition requests inconsistent relief.** The summary seeks suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer seek permanent deletion, with no investigation requirement or suspension endpoint. Decide whether the filing seeks temporary protection, a final destruction order, or distinct stages supported by distinct legal authority.

5. **Paragraph 4 and prayer (a)—Withdrawal has no duration.** Even apart from deletion, indefinite withdrawal could exceed the quoted 180-day limit. Specify the permissible duration and conditions for expiration, modification, or reinstatement.

6. **Filing date and paragraph 5—The chronology is impossible as written.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot rely on completed testing conducted on Days 9–14 of the same review period. Correct the dates or review-period reference and establish when the findings actually became available.

7. **Paragraph 8—The mitigation chronology compounds the problem.** Restrictions imposed “after the Evaluation” also could not already have occurred by Day 3 on the stated timeline. Provide dates and distinguish pre-mitigation testing from any subsequent assessment.

8. **Paragraph 2—Eligibility to petition and standing are undeveloped.** A shared interest in public safety may not satisfy applicable petition requirements or, if judicial review becomes necessary, constitutional standing requirements. Identify the relevant administrative eligibility rule and any concrete member exposure; do not assume administrative participation and court standing require the same showing.

9. **Paragraphs 3–4—Statutory coverage is not established.** The draft does not show that each Covered System meets the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system” or otherwise falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction. Address the statutory criteria, applicable thresholds, and any relevant exceptions.

10. **Cover sheet and paragraph 3(a)—The systems are not sufficiently identified.** “Its proprietary frontier AI models” is a category, not an operationally precise inventory. Identify model names, versions, deployment identifiers, and the criteria for including additional checkpoints or derivatives.

11. **Paragraphs 3(a), 5—The evaluation may not support the definition’s breadth.** The draft extends relief to all checkpoints, snapshots, and fine-tuned derivatives without showing that each shares the tested capability or risk. Establish a technical basis for grouping systems, or narrow the requested findings and relief.

12. **Paragraph 5—The central evidence is missing.** An unpublished report offered only on request leaves the Commission without the supporting record needed to evaluate an emergency application. Submit the report, relevant supporting materials, and an evaluator declaration, using any available confidential-filing procedures.

13. **Paragraph 5—“Third-party” does not establish credibility or independence.** Respondent can challenge the evaluator’s qualifications, funding, relationships, access, and methods. Disclose those matters and explain the evaluator’s relevant expertise and safeguards against bias.

14. **Paragraph 5—The claimed capability lacks test conditions and metrics.** “Autonomously carry out multi-step intrusions” leaves unanswered the success rate, number of trials, human assistance, tooling, credentials, target vulnerabilities, and whether testing involved simulations or operational environments. Supply those details and explain what “autonomously” means.

15. **Paragraphs 5–7—Tested configurations are not linked to deployed configurations.** A model tested with privileged access, removed safeguards, or unusual scaffolding may not demonstrate the capabilities available through public products. Identify the exact configurations tested and show how relevant users could reproduce the dangerous capability through the access routes alleged.

16. **Paragraphs 5–7—Intrusion capability is not itself proof of essential-service disruption.** The draft needs to connect the demonstrated behavior to reachable industrial systems, effective compromise, operational consequences, and public-safety injury. Address intervening barriers such as authentication, segmentation, operator controls, and specialized equipment requirements.

17. **Paragraphs 4, 7—The alleged timeline does not establish an “imminent” hazard.** Harm that “could” occur “within the next several years” is facially difficult to reconcile with an emergency imminent-hazard standard. Explain the governing interpretation of imminence and supply facts showing why the hazard is present or impending rather than merely possible.

18. **Paragraph 7—Likelihood and severity are unsupported.** The draft names serious possible outcomes but supplies no grounded account of threat actors, exposure, probability, or likely scale. Quantify where defensible, acknowledge uncertainty, and distinguish observed facts from projections.

19. **Paragraphs 6–7—The causal contribution of these systems is unclear.** Respondent may argue that the risk originates in malicious actors and existing infrastructure vulnerabilities, with comparable intrusion capabilities already available elsewhere. Explain how the Covered Systems materially increase the risk and how the proposed restrictions would reduce it; exclusivity need not be assumed.

20. **Paragraph 8—The mitigation account is unsourced.** “Petitioner understands” neither establishes what changed nor whether the changes cover every relevant product and integration. Cite reliable evidence of the restrictions, their implementation dates, coverage, and exceptions.

21. **Paragraph 8—Insufficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated.** The petition does not explain why tool restrictions and request screening fail to address the tested attack pathways. Provide post-mitigation testing or a supported technical explanation of the residual hazard, including any demonstrated bypasses.

22. **Paragraphs 7–9—The petition’s own theory supports less destructive measures.** If the hazard arises when outside users gain access, disabling that access could address the stated hazard without deleting the underlying models. Explain why deployment suspension, integration shutdowns, tool restrictions, access controls, or isolated storage would not suffice.

23. **Paragraphs 6, 9—Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary status concerns rights and access practices; it does not prove that no cloud provider, licensee, affiliate, contractor, or unauthorized party possesses a copy. Investigate custody and control rather than infer them from the licensing model.

24. **Paragraph 9—Deletion cannot be assumed to eliminate the hazard “with certainty.”** That claim requires proof that every relevant copy is covered and recoverable copies, reconstruction pathways, or substitutes cannot sustain the identified risk. Frame the remedy’s expected effects and limitations accurately instead of making an unsupported guarantee.

25. **Paragraphs 6, 9 and prayer (a)–(b)—The geographic scope contradicts the claimed complete solution.** The draft acknowledges facilities abroad but requests deletion only in the United States and withdrawal only from U.S. offerings. Explain how retained foreign copies and foreign services affect the hazard and redressability, while grounding any broader remedy in actual territorial and entity jurisdiction.

26. **Paragraph 3(a) and prayer—“Held by,” “stored,” and “offers” leave control gaps.** The language may treat respondent-controlled cloud copies, independently operated integrations, licensed copies, and affiliate-held assets differently without justification. Define possession, custody, control, and affected distribution channels, and explain what Respondent can legally and technically cause third parties to do.

27. **Paragraph 10—The basis for dispensing with prior notice is absent.** The draft identifies no authority for an ex parte order and no facts showing that notice itself would create unacceptable danger or defeat effective relief. Address the applicable emergency procedure, why expedited notice would be inadequate, and any safeguards the law requires.

28. **Paragraph 10—A hearing after deletion cannot meaningfully prevent erroneous destruction.** Permanent deletion before Respondent can contest the facts presents a substantial due-process objection, especially where a temporary suspension could preserve safety during adjudication. Distinguish any lawful immediate interim restriction from irreversible final relief and provide meaningful opportunities to contest the evidence and proposed remedy.

29. **Paragraphs 4, 10—Emergency action still requires a supported finding.** The quoted provision makes an imminent-hazard finding a condition of suspension; urgency does not replace that finding. Identify the applicable evidentiary standard and give the Commission a reasoned record addressing contrary evidence, mitigations, and uncertainty.

30. **Paragraphs 9–10 and prayer (b)—Deletion may destroy evidence needed for investigation and review.** Eliminating all checkpoints could prevent replication, independent evaluation, and examination of whether the order was justified. Address evidence-preservation duties and secure access arrangements, recognizing that retaining evidentiary copies would qualify the demand for total deletion.

31. **Paragraph 9—Commercial value raises objections the draft does not answer.** Respondent will emphasize irreversible property loss, proportionality, and potentially takings or other statutory and constitutional claims, whose strength depends on the governing law and facts. Acknowledge the burden and establish the legal and evidentiary justification rather than treating asset value as either an automatic bar or irrelevant.

32. **Paragraphs 6, 9 and prayer—Effects on customers and public safety are omitted.** Broad withdrawal could disrupt legitimate or safety-relevant uses and impose burdens on customers and integration partners. Assess those consequences and explain why the chosen scope and any transition arrangements are consistent with the asserted emergency.

33. **Paragraph 10 and prayer (a)–(b)—The implementation timeline is unclear and unsupported.** An order taking effect immediately does not specify when withdrawal must be completed, while the ten-day deletion deadline has no technical justification. Define milestones and explain both why compliance is feasible and how the hazard will be controlled during that period.

34. **Prayer (b)—“All copies” and “permanently delete” lack technical definitions.** The order does not address backups, disaster-recovery systems, distributed shards, cached weights, archival media, or materials capable of restoring a model. Define the covered artifacts and an achievable destruction standard, without unintentionally sweeping in unrelated records or protected evidence.

35. **Prayer (c)—Self-reporting is an inadequate verification plan.** A statement filed whenever deletion is complete has no fixed reporting deadline, specified contents, attestation requirement, or independent verification. Establish an inventory, compliance milestones, responsible-officer certification, and any legally authorized audit mechanism.

36. **Prayer—Indivisibility makes the entire request unnecessarily vulnerable.** Respondent can argue that the Commission cannot grant the requested “single order” because its deletion component exceeds the quoted authority, even if temporary suspension would otherwise be justified. Make relief severable and request a lawful interim alternative expressly.

37. **Caption, paragraphs 2, 5, 10, and signature block—Filing requirements remain unaddressed.** Depending on the Commission’s rules, the petition may need additional jurisdictional allegations, verification, declarations, service documents, counsel information, confidentiality motions, or a proposed order. Check those requirements and replace relative “Day” references with unambiguous dates and the relevant docket or review-period identifier.

**Highest-priority repairs:** correct the chronology and citation; submit the evidence; establish a current, post-mitigation imminent hazard; and separate any supportable temporary suspension request from permanent deletion, which needs independent authority and substantially stronger procedural protections.
